analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell prescription drugs to Medicare at prices the government negotiates.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees from June 2005 until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with three cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug manufacturers to make their drugs available to Medicare at prices negotiated by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, working with the Defense and Veterans Affairs departments. It would have backed that requirement by banning noncompliant manufacturers from federal contracts, set up an ombudsman to stop pharmacies from overcharging beneficiaries in areas with little competition, and repealed the Medicare Part D provision that bars the government from negotiating drug prices. It never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly 40 million older and disabled Americans, would have paid less for prescription drugs. Taxpayers would also have benefited, since Medicare picks up much of the drug bill through the Part D program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Each participating manufacturer would have to make covered outpatient drugs available to pharmacies, physicians, and Medicare providers at a price the HHS Secretary, in conjunction with the Defense and Veterans Affairs Secretaries, negotiates with the manufacturer, covering the full volume dispensed to Medicare beneficiaries.

The bill would strike subsection (i) of the Part D statute, the provision known as 'non-interference' that bars the government from interfering with negotiations between drug makers and private plans, thereby removing the legal shield that keeps Medicare out of price negotiations.
Manufacturers that do not comply would be debarred, meaning excluded from federal contracting and subcontracting for a period commensurate with the offense, giving the government real leverage.

The Secretary would have to set up a dispute-resolution mechanism, such as an ombudsman, to ensure drug resellers do not artificially raise prices above the negotiated level in low-competition areas like rural communities and do not collude on prices elsewhere.

Negotiators must take into account the goal of promoting the development of breakthrough drugs, and the Secretary would report to Congress annually on whether the act is reducing prices and protecting beneficiaries from discriminatory pricing.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose Medicare and federal health program sales would carry lower negotiated prices, with the indirect risk that reduced revenue slows investment in new drug development.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own drafters acknowledge the innovation tradeoff: the Secretary must weigh 'the goal of promoting the development of breakthrough drugs' when negotiating, an implicit admission that lower prices could reduce the revenue that funds research on new medicines.

The design is thin: it applies only to 'participating manufacturers,' defined as companies that contract with the United States to sell covered drugs, so its leverage rests on federal purchasing power and the debarment penalty rather than a comprehensive pricing system, and the bill text contains no estimate of savings or administrative cost.
Debarment is a blunt enforcement tool; excluding a major manufacturer from federal contracts could disrupt drug supply for veterans and service members before it lowered anyone's prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the potential benefit is large: the same drugs the government already buys for veterans and service members at negotiated federal prices would be available to Medicare at negotiated rates, and the repeal of the non-interference clause removes the specific legal barrier Congress put there in 2003. The costs fall on a concentrated industry, with a genuine but speculative secondary risk to drug innovation that the bill itself tries to manage by carving out breakthrough drugs. The bill's design is skeletal, however, and there is no fiscal estimate in the record of how much it would have saved or cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees in May 2005 and then to their Health subcommittees in June, and it never received a markup, hearing vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Price Negotiation Act on May 26, 2005, joined by three Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, for the provisions in its jurisdiction, to the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction.
In early and mid-June 2005, both committees referred the bill to their Health subcommittees, where the action history ends.
No further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so the bill died in subcommittee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were better off: Medicare's bar on price negotiation stayed on the books, and the new Part D drug benefit that took effect in 2006 continued to route seniors' prescriptions through private plans at market prices with no government negotiation.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 26, 2005, to require negotiated Medicare drug prices and repeal the Part D non-interference clause.

for.name: 3 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Raul Grijalva and Maurice Hinchey.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 26, 2005, sent it to its Health Subcommittee on June 6, 2005, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Additional committee of referral with jurisdiction over Medicare
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 26, 2005, sent it to its Health Subcommittee on June 17, 2005, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturer industry
against.role: Industry whose products the bill would price-regulate
against.what_they_did: Opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices during this era, defending the non-interference clause this bill would repeal; opposition never had to materialize on this bill because it never left subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled House took no action; no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to sell to Medicare at government-negotiated prices across their entire Medicare volume, backed by a federal contracting ban for refusers, and would repeal the statutory clause that currently bars Medicare from negotiating. For seniors, the industry's preservation of non-negotiated prices means paying more at the pharmacy.

Pharmacies would buy drugs at the lower negotiated price but would face an ombudsman mechanism policing artificial markups in low-competition rural areas and price collusion elsewhere. The bill lowers their acquisition cost while capping their ability to charge beneficiaries more than the negotiated price.
